beats.narration_text: Hello, I'm Vineet S.. The biggest model is rarely the right model. Every A I product trades quality against speed and cost, and product managers make that call. Here is how to choose between models without guessing.

props.segment: AI Product Cost, Latency & Model Selection
props.command: How do I choose the right AI model for my product?

Test models on your own cases

beats.narration_text: Always pick the cheapest model, good enough for the job. Bigger models are usually smarter, slower and costlier. The right choice depends on the task, and you find it by testing, not by reputation.

beats.narration_text: Here are the five levers. Quality. Response speed. Token usage. Infrastructure capacity. And cost. Improving one usually moves another, so model selection is a balancing act.

Cost follows tokens. Providers usually charge for the tokens you send in and the tokens the model writes back, and output often costs more. Long prompts, long documents and long answers all add up. Multiply the cost of one request by your expected daily traffic, and check the result against what a user is worth.

layers.title: Cost per request
layers.sub: Input plus output, at your prices

beats.narration_text: Speed has two parts: how long until the first words appear, and how long the full answer takes. Streaming makes a wait feel shorter. Larger models are usually slower, and long outputs take longer. If the user is waiting, for example in a chat, speed is part of the product, not a technical detail.

Infrastructure capacity is the hidden constraint. Providers set rate limits, and traffic spikes can cause slowdowns or errors. If you host models yourself, you need enough hardware at peak, not just on average. Plan for peaks, add fallbacks, and know what happens when a model is unavailable.

layers.title: Self-hosting
layers.sub: Hardware must cover peak, not average

layers.title: Fallbacks
layers.sub: Know what happens when it is down

beats.narration_text: You have tactics to balance all this. Use a smaller model for easy tasks and a larger one for hard ones. Route each request to the right model. Shorten prompts, cache repeated answers, and limit output length. Often a mix beats any single model.

So how do you choose? Define the quality bar and the latency and cost budgets first. Test two or three candidate models on your own real cases, with the same rubric. Compare quality, speed and cost side by side. Pick the cheapest that clears the bar, and re-check as new models arrive.

beats.narration_text: So, model selection. Balance quality, speed, tokens, capacity and cost. Test on your own cases. And pick the cheapest model that clears your bar.
